central_conflict: Melos must return within three days to face death, or his friend, held as a hostage, will die. Dangerous delays and his temptation to give up test his promise and their trust.

key_scenes.scene: Melos openly criticizes the ruler for killing suspected enemies without fair trials and is sentenced to death.
key_scenes.why: This establishes the ruler's cruelty and the serious danger facing Melos.

key_scenes.scene: Melos receives three days to attend his sister's wedding while his friend stays as a hostage.
key_scenes.why: The deadline and the friend's danger make keeping the promise a matter of life and death.

key_scenes.scene: After the wedding, Melos races back, but dangerous water and then attackers delay and weaken him.
key_scenes.why: The obstacles make his return uncertain and increase the pressure of the deadline.

key_scenes.scene: Near collapse, Melos is tempted to give up and let his friend die.
key_scenes.why: This is his lowest point, when keeping his promise becomes an inner struggle as well as a difficult journey.

key_scenes.scene: Trust helps Melos revive and decide again to keep his promise.
key_scenes.why: His renewed resolve connects the theme of trust to his effort to return.

key_scenes.scene: Melos reaches the city just before the execution begins, and his friend is freed.
key_scenes.why: The last-minute arrival answers the central question of whether he will keep his promise in time.

key_scenes.scene: The ruler is changed by the loyalty and mutual trust of Melos and his friend.
key_scenes.why: Their trust affects the ruler and gives the ending meaning beyond the friend's escape from death.

engaging_progression: The death sentence, three-day deadline, and hostage arrangement make the reader wonder whether Melos can return in time. Dangerous water and attackers slow him down and leave him weak, until he is tempted to abandon his friend. His renewed trust turns that low point into a final effort toward the city.
climax_and_aftertaste: The climax is Melos's arrival just before the execution begins, followed by his friend's release. The ruler's change should let the ending move from danger and doubt to relief and a sense of the strength of mutual trust.

brief_text:
Storyline: Melos must return to face death in time to save his friend.

Write a 300–350-word story in simple, mainly third-person English for A2 learners. Keep the kingdom setting. Use Melos as the only personal name; refer to others by their roles.

Begin with Melos openly criticizing the ruler for killing suspected enemies without fair trials. The ruler sentences him to death but gives him three days to attend his sister's wedding. His friend stays as a hostage and will die if Melos does not return in time.

After the wedding, Melos races back. Dangerous water and then attackers delay him and leave him weak. Make the time pressure grow through these obstacles. At his lowest point, he nearly collapses and is tempted to stop, even though his friend would die. Keep this difficult choice: trust helps him recover his resolve and continue.

The climax is his arrival just before the execution begins. His friend is freed, and the ruler is changed by their loyalty and mutual trust. End with relief and a sense of the strength of trust. Wedding details and descriptions of the obstacles may be brief, but keep the promise, the temptation, and the renewed effort.
